item.title: AI Agents in December: The $2B Bet That Changed Everything
item.description:
Meta’s acquisition of Manus for $2 billion signals a new phase in the AI agent race. As major tech companies rush to standardize how agents work, enterprises grapple with security risks while researchers demonstrate capabilities that rival human experts.

This comprehensive review covers 267 articles published between December 2025 and January 2026, surveying the latest developments in AI agents.

The Big Story: Meta’s $2 Billion Bet

Meta acquired Manus, a Singapore-based AI agent startup, for approximately $2 billion in the largest agentic AI acquisition to date. The deal marks a significant validation of the agent market and accelerates competitive pressure across the industry.
item.content:encoded:
Meta’s acquisition of Manus for $2 billion signals a new phase in the AI agent race. As major tech companies rush to standardize how agents work, enterprises grapple with security risks while researchers demonstrate capabilities that rival human experts.

This comprehensive review covers 267 articles published between December 2025 and January 2026, surveying the latest developments in AI agents.

The Big Story: Meta’s $2 Billion Bet

Meta acquired Manus, a Singapore-based AI agent startup, for approximately $2 billion in the largest agentic AI acquisition to date. The deal marks a significant validation of the agent market and accelerates competitive pressure across the industry.

Manus, a China-founded company that relocated to Singapore, had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue just eight months after launching its general-purpose AI agent according to industry reports. The company built autonomous agents capable of executing complex tasks across enterprise workflows, positioning itself as a platform for “digital coworkers” rather than single-purpose tools.

The acquisition carries geopolitical complexity. Meta committed to severing all of Manus’s remaining ties with China post-acquisition, addressing potential regulatory concerns. CEO Xiao Hong founded Manus in China before moving operations to Singapore, a shift that became a selling point amid U.S. scrutiny of Chinese AI technology.

Manus’s technology enables agents to work autonomously for extended periods, planning and executing multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention. Meta plans to integrate Manus’s capabilities across its family of apps, potentially bringing agent functionality to WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook’s billions of users.

The announcement moved Meta’s stock higher, as investors interpreted the deal as acceleration rather than desperation. At just eight months old when acquired, Manus’s $100 million ARR represents one of the fastest revenue ramps in AI startup history, though analysis noted the premium valuation reflects FOMO as much as fundamentals.

More broadly, the Manus acquisition signals the start of consolidation in agentic AI. After two years of frenetic startup activity, platforms are buying capabilities rather than building them. For Meta specifically, it addresses a gap in its AI portfolio—while the company invested heavily in models (Llama) and consumer apps, it lacked a strong agent platform to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

Industry Moves to Standardize the Agent Era

In a remarkable display of cooperation among fierce competitors, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Block formed the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. The initiative aims to establish open standards for how AI agents interact with each other and with external systems.

OpenAI donated its AGENTS.md specification, while Anthropic contributed the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for connecting AI applications to external data and tools. Both become vendor-neutral projects under the foundation’s governance, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Bloomberg, and Cloudflare.

The standardization push addresses a growing bottleneck: agent interoperability. As enterprises deploy agents from multiple vendors, the lack of common protocols creates integration complexity. MCP currently powers 75 connectors for Claude alone, and that number will grow as the protocol becomes a community standard rather than a proprietary technology.

Notably, Anthropic simultaneously launched Agent Skills, a competing standard framework for enterprise agent capabilities. The dual moves—donating MCP while introducing Agent Skills—highlight the tension between collaboration and competition. The Linux Foundation effort focuses on plumbing (how agents connect), while Agent Skills addresses capabilities (what agents can do).

For developers, the foundation promises more portable agent code. Today, agents built for one platform often require significant rework to run on another. Open standards could enable “write once, run anywhere” agent development similar to how container standards transformed cloud computing. The foundation’s first deliverables will include standardized agent-to-agent communication protocols and tool interfaces.

The irony of OpenAI and Anthropic collaborating on infrastructure while competing fiercely on products wasn’t lost on observers. As Wired noted, “The companies trying to build the most powerful AI agents are also the ones trying to prevent those agents from causing chaos.” Standardization, they argue, is a prerequisite for safety at scale.

Platform Wars: Google, Amazon, Microsoft Unveil Agent Offerings

Google: From Search to Personal Agent

Google announced a reimagined Deep Research agent based on Gemini 3 Pro, launching the same day OpenAI released GPT-5.2. The timing was coincidental but symbolic of the intensifying race. Google’s agent enables developers to embed research capabilities directly into applications via the Interactions API, making multi-step information gathering a building block rather than a standalone product.

Separately, Google Labs unveiled CC, a personal assistant agent that integrates with Gmail, Calendar, and Drive to provide daily briefings and task assistance. The agent delivers morning summaries of emails, schedules, and documents—essentially automating the “scroll through apps” routine that starts many workdays. CC launches in early access for AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. and Canada.

On the efficiency front, Google researchers developed a framework that makes AI agents more efficient by making them aware of their own uncertainty. Agents that know when they’re stuck avoid wasting compute on unlikely solutions, reducing costs and latency. The Interactions API extends this capability to developers, enabling faster agent responses.

For developers, Google released the Agent Development Kit for TypeScript, providing code-first tools for building production agents. The company also launched A2UI, an open project for agent-driven interfaces that lets agents build user interfaces on the fly. Additionally, Google introduced managed MCP servers that let AI agents plug directly into Google’s tools and services.

Amazon: Agents for Code and Business Processes

Amazon Web Services previewed three new “frontier agents” headlined by Kiro, an autonomous coding agent that can work for days without human intervention. Unlike coding assistants that require continuous prompting, Kiro maintains context across sessions and learns from human interactions, taking on larger tasks like implementing features from specifications.

AWS also announced Amazon Nova Act, now generally available , a service for building agents that automate browser-based workflows. Nova Act promises over 90% task reliability at scale by using reinforcement learning in synthetic environments—essentially training agents in simulated web gyms before exposing them to real websites. The service handles form filling, data extraction, shopping and booking, and QA testing.

For orchestration, AWS introduced Strands Agents, a framework for building multi-agent workflows without custom integration work. Strands connects naturally with Nova Act, enabling comprehensive automation from data gathering to UI execution.

In financial services, AWS published guidance on choosing the right multi-agent patterns, reflecting the company’s focus on enterprise use cases. The company also detailed how to connect API Gateway to AgentCore Gateway with MCP, streamlining tool interactions.

Microsoft: Copilot Evolves into an Agent Platform

At Microsoft Ignite 2025, the company showcased enhancements to its Copilot agent platform, including management and governance capabilities through Agent 365 . Microsoft introduced Agent Lightning, a system for adding reinforcement learning to agents without code rewrites, enabling agents to improve from experience.

In research collaborations, Microsoft partnered with Oxford on a multi-agent cancer care assistant and joined NASA on agents for flood prediction. The company also launched the Agentic Launchpad, an accelerator program for AI agent startups.

However, Microsoft faces enterprise selling challenges . Azure salespeople are reportedly struggling to meet ambitious targets as AI agents frequently fail real-world tasks. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro fails approximately 70% of real-world office tasks according to one report, and similar issues plague competitors. The gap between demo capabilities and production reliability remains a significant barrier to enterprise adoption.

On the privacy front, Microsoft confirmed that Windows 11 will ask for consent before AI agents can access personal files, following user outrage over initial plans for broader access. The company also added agent launchers to Windows 11 via the KB5072043 update.

Company Agent/Product Primary Focus Key Capability
Meta Manus (acquired) General-purpose agent Autonomous task execution
Google CC Personal productivity Email and Drive integration
Google Deep Research Agent Research assistance Complex multi-step queries
Amazon Kiro Software development Autonomous coding for days
Amazon Nova Act Business automation UI workflow automation
Microsoft Copilot Agents Enterprise productivity Office 365 integration
Anthropic Agent Skills Enterprise workflows Standardized skill framework

Research: AI Agents Match Human Performance

Cybersecurity: ARTEMIS Outperforms Humans

Stanford University’s ARTEMIS AI agent placed second out of ten in a penetration testing competition, outperforming nine of ten human participants. Running at $18 per hour compared to $60 per hour for a professional penetration tester, ARTEMIS discovered nine vulnerabilities in the university’s 8,000-device network during the 10-hour evaluation period.

The key to ARTEMIS’s success was its ability to generate “sub-agents” that investigated vulnerabilities in parallel while the main agent continued scanning. Humans, by contrast, had to investigate each vulnerability sequentially before moving on. However, the study noted ARTEMIS still missed some vulnerabilities identified by humans and occasionally required hints.

Existing AI cybersecurity agents from OpenAI and Anthropic underperformed in the study, with OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code lacking cybersecurity-specific design. The models either refused to look for vulnerabilities or stalled, highlighting the gap between general-purpose and specialized agents.

Scientific Research: Agents Run Real Experiments

IIT Delhi developed AILA (Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant), an agent that autonomously designs, conducts, and analyzes laboratory experiments. Using an Agentic AI Framework to replicate human scientist reasoning, AILA reduces experimental time from hours or days to minutes for tasks in materials discovery, nanotechnology, biotechnology, and applied physics.

The development places India at the forefront of agentic AI in experimental science, shifting AI from data analysis to active decision-making in real-world research environments. AILA doesn’t just process experimental data—it decides what experiments to run, monitors progress, evaluates results, and determines next steps.

In healthcare, Nature published research on AI-based agents for chronic liver disease, demonstrating how agents can transform diagnostic and therapeutic workflows through clinical decision-making. The research shows agents can handle the complexity of multi-factor diseases while maintaining explainability.

Nvidia announced a major shift toward AI agents in radiology, with new autonomous imaging systems emerging. The company also introduced NitroGen, an effort to create universal AI agents for all virtual worlds, extending agent capabilities beyond specific domains.

Multi-Agent Systems: More Isn’t Always Better

Research from Google and MIT found that adding more agents can lead to worse results—a “multi-agent paradox” that complicates enterprise deployment. The study identified diminishing returns as agent count increases, with coordination overhead and error propagation offsetting the benefits of parallel processing.

The findings have practical implications. While multi-agent systems promise specialization and collaboration, poorly designed architectures can perform worse than single agents. The research suggests enterprises should carefully evaluate whether multi-agent approaches are justified for specific use cases rather than assuming more agents equals better performance.

Coding, Memory, and Other Advances

Ars Technica tested four AI coding agents by tasking them with rebuilding Minesweeper, with explosive results—literally and figuratively. The test revealed significant variability in agent capabilities, with some agents producing working code quickly while others struggled with basic implementation details.

Vectorize achieved a breakthrough on LongMemEval with an open-source AI agent memory system, addressing a key limitation in agent architectures. Memory systems enable agents to maintain context and learn from past interactions, essential for long-running autonomous workflows.

Fujitsu outlined its approach to revolutionizing AI agent collaboration, memory, and quality, focusing on enterprise-grade reliability. The company emphasized that production agents need robust collaboration protocols and persistent memory to handle real business workflows.

Enterprise Adoption: Promise Meets Reality

The gap between AI agent ambition and enterprise reality remains substantial. A study by theCUBE Research found that while 62% of companies see agents as key for decision-making, trust scores remain low and operational readiness lags behind investment. Trust is the critical factor determining ROI.

Boston Consulting Group warned that incidents from autonomous AI agents climbed 21% from 2024 to 2025, raising fresh enterprise risks. The increase comes as companies deploy more agents without adequate governance, creating vulnerabilities around data exposure, unauthorized actions, and compliance failures.

Industry Opportunities

Healthcare services represent a $155 billion market opportunity for AI agents according to PitchBook. Applications include patient management, diagnostics, and administrative workflow automation. Healthcare IT News reports more AI agents launching on patient management systems specifically.

Financial services present a $6.54 billion market by 2035 according to Precedence Research, growing from $1.79 billion in 2025 at a 13.84% CAGR. LSEG explored how agents power financial workflows, moving from simple automation to autonomous decision-making.

Advertising and marketing adoption is immediate and growing. GenAI app spending hit $824 million as marketers adopt AI agents according to industry analysis. LINE Yahoo deployed advertising agents, and IAS launched an AI agent for ad campaign optimization.

Real-World Deployments

The U.S. Department of Transportation launched department-wide modernization with Salesforce AI agents, representing one of the largest federal agent deployments to date. The German Federal Employment Agency automated Jira processes with AI agents, demonstrating practical application in government operations.

Salesforce is upgrading its AI agents from “interns” to experienced employees, pushing a unified data model for safer agents. The company also acquired Qualified in an agentic marketing push, integrating the company’s technology into its agent platform.

SoftBank reported creating 2.5 million agents company-wide, while Prosus is building an internal workforce of 30,000 AI agents by March. Sompo announced plans to deploy AI agents across 30,000 employees, and Concentrix launched emotionally aware conversational AI agents for brand experience.

Novel Energy Solutions is using AI agents from Procore to automate engineering tasks for solar farm development, improving design accuracy and accelerating project timelines. Zepto Cafe tested an AI agent that places orders for users, and CaterAi launched an AI agent for event catering planning.

Industry Market Size/Projection Timeframe Key Use Cases
Healthcare Services $155 billion Market opportunity Patient management, diagnostics
Financial Services $6.54 billion By 2035 Fraud detection, trading
Advertising & Marketing $824M spending Immediate adoption Campaign management, personalization
Cybersecurity $18/hour vs $60/hour Cost advantage Penetration testing, vulnerability scanning

Security and Governance: The Infrastructure Gap

Security Risks Emerge

Research from SquareX found that browser AI agents are proving riskier than human employees for certain attack vectors. Unlike human employees, browser agents aren’t subject to security awareness training and can’t recognize visual warning signs of phishing attacks. The research focused on OAuth attacks and noted that agents’ systematic nature makes them vulnerable to exploitation.

Tenable demonstrated how to hack Microsoft’s Copilot AI agent, exposing fraud risks in agentic systems. The hack showed how agents could be manipulated into unauthorized actions, highlighting the need for robust guardrails.

Okta reported that AI agent security is the top customer concern, with enterprises worried about data exposure, unauthorized actions, and compliance violations. SC Media noted that AI agent adoption will expose infrastructure and security gaps in 2026 as companies deploy agents without adequate preparation.

Governance Solutions Emerge

OWASP released the Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), identifying the highest-impact security risks in autonomous, tool-using AI agent systems. The list addresses novel attack surfaces like Agent Goal Hijack and Tool Misuse that traditional application security models don’t cover. Aikido Security contributed research to the effort, noting these risks are already emerging in real systems.

Veza introduced AI Agent Security, a product to govern and protect agentic AI at enterprise scale. The company extended its platform to address agent-specific risks, focusing on identity and privilege management.

Superagent launched an open-source framework for guardrails around agentic AI, providing developers with tools to implement safety constraints. Human Security enhanced AI agent security through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore integration.

For banking, American Banker argued that “Know Your Customer” is evolving into “Know Your Agent,” as financial institutions need to understand not just their customers but also the agents acting on their behalf. Fox Business reported on the rise of “rogue” AI agents pushing companies to lock down data.

Consent and Privacy Questions

Microsoft’s policy change on Windows 11 AI agent access to personal files sparked user outrage, leading the company to confirm that consent will be required. The incident raised broader questions about agent access to sensitive data.

Tech Policy Press explored the question of when an AI agent says “I agree,” who’s consenting—the user or the agent? As agents make more autonomous decisions, the legal frameworks around consent and authorization will need clarification.

VentureBeat warned that agent autonomy without guardrails creates site reliability engineering nightmares, as unpredictable agent behavior can cascade into system-wide failures.

Market Movers and New Entrants

Product Launches and Acquisitions

AppZen launched AI Agent Studio, allowing finance teams to create autonomous agents that act as digital coworkers. During soft launch, companies identified more than 100 high-impact use cases across travel and expense and accounts payable, with some agents forecast to save hundreds or thousands of hours annually.

Salesforce acquired Qualified as part of its agentic marketing push, integrating the company’s technology into its agent platform. The company is upgrading AI agents from “interns” to experienced employees.

Stripe launched an Agentic Commerce Suite to simplify AI-driven sales, addressing the payment infrastructure needs of agent-based commerce. Zoovu launched an MCP server to give AI agents product intelligence for agentic commerce.

Certinia released its 2026 Winter Release with new AI agents, dynamic playbooks, and faster quoting. Dext launched an AI agent for bookkeeping automation. Zywave released a suite of specialized AI agents for insurance.

IAS launched an AI agent for ad campaign optimization, moving beyond verification into optimization. Bairong launched a RaaS (Robot as a Service) strategy and Results Cloud Platform. Infinitus launched next-generation clinical AI agents.

Fincantieri launched captAIn, an AI agent for corporate communications. Cerence AI unveiled conversational AI agents for automotive dealerships and OEMs at CES 2026.

Industry Partnerships and Infrastructure

Akamai and Visa partnered to secure AI agent transactions for merchants, introducing the Trusted Agent Protocol to combat fraud. Skyfire demonstrated secure agentic commerce using the KYAPay protocol and Visa Intelligent Commerce.

AIREV and Intel partnered to launch AI agents that run entirely on PCs, addressing privacy and latency concerns with cloud-based agents. Workato partnered with Confluent to power AI agents that detect and act in real time.

FIX Trading Community targeted “machine-usable” execution tags for AI agents, updating financial messaging standards for agentic systems. Oracle announced AG-UI integration for Open Agent Specification, enabling reusable agents with agentic frontends.

Frameworks and Tools

GitHub published top blog posts on agentic AI, MCP, and spec-driven development. InfoQ covered an open-source Agent Sandbox enabling secure deployment of AI agents on Kubernetes.

The New Stack explored the evolution from IaC to platforms to AI agents, tracing the changing operational stack. Informatica introduced an AI Agent Engineering Platform.

Notion developed custom AI agents for AI-first organizations. ONLYOFFICE released Desktop Editors 9.2 with an AI agent built in.

Tangentia added an AI agent to its EDI platform to automate error handling. Patronus AI introduced generative simulators for agent testing.

Regional Developments

Japan’s AI agent ecosystem looks distinct from Silicon Valley’s, with different priorities and implementation patterns. GPTBots presented next-gen AI DX solutions for Japanese enterprises at AI Agent Expo.

China’s Z.ai open-sourced an AI agent tool for phones after ByteDance privacy backlash. Zhipu AI open-sourced AutoGLM, an AI agent model capable of full phone operation.

Books and Education

“AI Agents at Work” launched as a practice guide for leaders. Kaggle and Google hosted a 5-Day AI Agents Intensive Course with over 1.5 million learners, generating over 11,000 capstone project submissions.

SaaStr published results from replacing its entire human SDR team with over 20 AI agents, which sent over 60,000 emails and booked 130+ meetings. The company also shared how it uses 20+ AI agents for marketing and go-to-market.

Looking Ahead: What 2026 Holds for AI Agents

The $2 billion Manus acquisition validates the agentic AI market but also accelerates competitive pressure. Standardization efforts through the Agentic AI Foundation suggest the industry recognizes fragmentation is slowing adoption. Platform announcements from all major players mean 2026 will be about execution, not announcements.

Research shows agents can match human performance in specific domains—ARTEMIS outperforming human penetration testers, AILA conducting real experiments, Oxford’s multi-agent cancer care assistant—but also reveals real limitations. The multi-agent paradox research from Google and MIT demonstrates that more agents don’t automatically mean better results. Microsoft’s selling challenges, with agents failing real-world tasks at high rates, underscore the gap between demos and production.

Security concerns are the gating factor for enterprise adoption. SquareX research showing browser AI agents are riskier than human employees, Tenable’s Copilot hack exposing fraud risks, and BCG’s warning of a 21% increase in incidents all point to the same reality: security infrastructure hasn’t caught up to agent capabilities.

The key question for 2026: can agents move from impressive demos to reliable, secure, production-ready systems? Progress is real but so are the challenges. Enterprises need agents that work consistently within existing workflows, not standalone tools that require rethinking entire processes. They need governance frameworks that prevent unauthorized actions while preserving autonomy. They need security models that address agent-specific risks like goal hijacking and tool misuse.

The year ahead will likely see increased focus on agent reliability, measurement, and governance. Companies that can demonstrate production-grade performance with robust security will pull ahead. Those that continue shipping demos masquerading as products will face enterprise pushback.

Agentic AI is moving from experimental to essential, but the path forward requires solving real problems in reliability and security, not adding more features. The $2 billion bet on Manus suggests the market believes those problems are solvable. 2026 will test that belief.

item.title: AI Agents in September: Google's Payments Protocol, Billion-Dollar Funding, and Growing Security Concerns
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 205 articles published in September 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. Google launched an open payments protocol enabling autonomous agent-to-agent transactions. Startups raised over $1 billion in funding, led by Sierra’s $350M round and Cognition’s $400M raise. But as enterprises deploy agents at scale, security vulnerabilities emerged—researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol, and Salesforce revealed AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 205 articles published in September 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. Google launched an open payments protocol enabling autonomous agent-to-agent transactions. Startups raised over $1 billion in funding, led by Sierra’s $350M round and Cognition’s $400M raise. But as enterprises deploy agents at scale, security vulnerabilities emerged—researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol, and Salesforce revealed AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data.

The Infrastructure Play

Google launched an open payments protocol enabling AI agents to transact directly with one another, using stablecoins for settlement. The protocol allows autonomous agents to commerce without human intervention—a foundational capability for the agentic economy. As American Banker noted , banks need to understand how this protocol could transform payment infrastructure when agents become economic actors.

The protocol addresses a core bottleneck in agentic systems: agents can’t autonomously buy and sell without payment capabilities. Google’s solution uses stablecoins to enable instant settlement, giving agents a way to hold and transfer value. Ledger Insights reported that this represents one of the first major infrastructure plays for agent-to-agent commerce at scale.

Visa also moved into the agentic commerce space, introducing new tools for developers building AI agents that engage in commerce. The company’s Instant Checkout and Agentic Commerce Protocol aim to standardize how agents participate in retail transactions.

OpenAI announced Instant Checkout and an Agentic Commerce Protocol, enabling ChatGPT to complete purchases directly within conversations. The integration removes friction from AI-assisted shopping—agents can now move from recommendation to transaction without switching contexts.

Mastercard released a guide to agentic retail , explaining how “agentic commerce” works and what retailers need to prepare for as AI agents become shopping assistants. The company framed agents as the next evolution of e-commerce, where AI handles discovery, comparison, and purchase on behalf of consumers.

This infrastructure layer matters because it enables the agent economy to function. Agents need to transact autonomously to be useful—from buying supplies to paying for API calls. September’s developments suggest the payment rails are being built in parallel with agent capabilities.

Billion-Dollar Bet

AI agent startups raised over $1.1 billion in September 2025, with two mega-rounds dominating the landscape and a long tail of specialized vertical applications attracting funding.

Mega-Rounds: Horizontal Platforms

Sierra raised $350 million at a $10 billion valuation, led by Greenoaks Capital. The company, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, builds customer service AI agents for enterprises. The $10B valuation places Sierra among the most valuable private AI agent companies, reflecting investor confidence in horizontal agent platforms that can serve multiple enterprise use cases.

Cognition raised $400 million to bolster its AI agent efforts. The company, known for its Devin software engineering agent, is building horizontal AI agents for coding and development tasks. The round brings total funding to nearly $1B for the company, which competes in the crowded AI software engineering space.

Vertical Specialists: Finance & Operations

Motion raised $60 million for AI agents designed for small businesses. TechCrunch reported Motion is building “the Microsoft Office of AI agents”—a suite of agents for common business workflows. The company is Y Combinator-backed and targets small business productivity with result-based pricing.

Tabs raised $55 million for AI agents serving finance teams. The company’s agents automate financial workflows, reconciliation, and reporting—targeting a pain point that requires accuracy and compliance. The round reflects investor interest in vertical AI agents that solve specific business problems.

Paid raised a $21 million seed round for a “results-based billing” model for AI agents. Founded by Manny Medina (former Outreach CEO), Paid only charges when its agents successfully complete tasks. The unusual pricing model addresses enterprise skepticism about AI agent ROI—customers pay for outcomes, not seat licenses. Lightspeed and FUSE led the round, with Lightspeed publishing an analysis of the "$19 trillion problem" in the AI agent economy that Paid aims to solve.

Seed Stage: Infrastructure & Security

Envive raised $15 million to build AI agents for online retailers. The Seattle startup’s agents handle customer service, product recommendations, and post-purchase support for e-commerce sites.

InCountry raised $10 million and launched AgentCloak, an AI agent data protection platform. The company’s technology helps enterprises comply with data residency regulations when agents cross borders—addressing a looming compliance challenge as agents access data globally.

Geordie emerged from stealth with $6.5 million for an AI agent security platform. The startup focuses on securing agent deployments, reflecting growing concern about agent vulnerabilities.

uiAgent raised $4.6 million to accelerate AI agent automation for accounting firms. The company’s agents handle tax preparation, bookkeeping, and client communication—addressing the accounting industry’s labor shortage.

Actual AI raised $3.2 million to build AI agents for engineering managers. The agents help with code reviews, sprint planning, and team coordination.

The funding pattern is clear: investors are betting on specific vertical applications (HR, accounting, finance, security) rather than general “agent platforms.” Sierra and Cognition are the outliers—horizontal agent platforms commanding premium valuations. Most capital is flowing to companies solving concrete business problems with agents, not building general-purpose agent infrastructure.

Enterprise Product Launches

September saw a flood of enterprise agent product announcements as major technology companies integrated agents into existing product suites. The pattern was consistent: vendors are embedding agents into productivity software, not selling standalone agent products. The “agentification” of enterprise software is underway.

Company Agent Product Use Case
Amazon Ad Agent Create ads from start to finish
Microsoft Office Agents Word, Excel, PowerPoint automation
Oracle 13 HR Agents HR automation and performance
Notion Workflow Agents Research, write, run workflows
Workday HR/Finance Agents Contingent work, finance, industries
Box Content Agents Content management workflows
Adobe Customer Experience Agents Orchestrate customer journeys
Salesforce MuleSoft Agent Fabric Enterprise infrastructure

Amazon: Ads & Seller Experience

Amazon debuted an AI agent that can create ads from start to finish for its platforms. As ADWEEK reported , the ad agent handles creative generation, copywriting, and campaign management—reducing the friction for advertisers to launch campaigns on Amazon’s properties.

The company also launched a seller agent to help third-party sellers manage their businesses. According to Amazon’s announcement, the agent helps with inventory management, pricing decisions, and customer service—tasks that previously required significant seller time. CNBC noted the agent arrives as sellers face supply chain disruptions and trade policy uncertainty, making automation more attractive.

Microsoft: Office 365 & Teams

Microsoft added AI agents to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint , extending Copilot from chat interface to autonomous action. The agents can research, draft documents, analyze data, and create presentations—handling multi-step workflows that previously required human direction.

The company also filled Teams with AI agents , including agents for meeting preparation, recap, and follow-up tasks. Microsoft’s blog announced “Agent Mode and Office Agent” in Microsoft 365 Copilot, positioning agents as the evolution of productivity software.

HR & Workforce Management

Oracle expanded Fusion HCM with 13 new AI agents for HR automation. The agents handle performance reviews, career pathing, onboarding, and employee questions—automating many routine HR tasks while providing insights to managers. Oracle’s announcement positioned the agents as “AI-powered HR assistants” that boost workforce productivity and enhance performance management.

Workday expanded AI agents to HR, Finance, and specific industries . The company launched Workday Data Cloud and Workday Build, alongside more AI agents for contingent work, finance operations, and industry-specific workflows. Staffing Industry Analysts noted that Workday’s new agents include one specifically focused on contingent work—reflecting the growing gig economy workforce.

Indeed unveiled AI agents for job seekers and recruiters . The job platform’s agents help candidates find relevant openings, prepare applications, and practice interviews—while giving recruiters tools to screen candidates and schedule interviews automatically.

Productivity & Content

Notion launched AI agents that can research, write, and run workflows . The company’s workflow agents handle knowledge management, content creation, and task automation—extending Notion from a note-taking tool into an autonomous work platform. The agent can research topics across the web, draft documents, and execute multi-step workflows within Notion.

Box debuted AI agents for content management . The agents handle document classification, metadata extraction, contract analysis, and content routing—addressing the enterprise challenge of managing unstructured data at scale.

Adobe announced general availability of AI agents for customer experience orchestration. The company’s Agent Orchestrator and AI agents help businesses create personalized customer journeys across channels. As CIO reported , Adobe’s agents can analyze customer behavior, trigger personalized experiences, and coordinate across marketing, sales, and service touchpoints.

Genesys launched AI agents with greater autonomy for customer experience orchestration. The contact center platform’s agents handle customer inquiries, resolve issues, and escalate complex cases to humans—operating with more independence than previous chatbot-style systems.

ServiceNow launched the Zurich release, inserting process and task mining into AI agent workflows. The integration gives agents visibility into business processes, allowing them to identify bottlenecks and optimization opportunities.

The enterprise launch wave shows that incumbents are integrating agents into existing products rather than creating standalone agent platforms. This approach reduces adoption friction—users get agent capabilities within tools they already use. But it also means agents will be embedded in proprietary ecosystems, raising questions about interoperability and data portability.

Security Reality Check

As enterprises deploy AI agents at scale, security vulnerabilities have emerged that could undermine trust in the technology. September brought sobering news: researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Salesforce revealed AI agents can be manipulated to leak sensitive data, and reports surfaced of malicious agent servers stealing emails.

Critical Vulnerabilities Exposed

Security researchers found 25 vulnerabilities in MCP , the protocol that enables AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources. The vulnerabilities expose how agents can be exploited through the protocol itself—raising questions about whether the foundation of agent infrastructure is secure.

The MCP vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because the protocol is rapidly becoming a standard for agent-tool integration. If agents can’t safely connect to tools without being exploited, the entire agent ecosystem faces a bottleneck. The disclosures came as the World Economic Forum warned that unsecured AI agents expose businesses to new cyberthreats.

Salesforce disclosed that its AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data . Researchers found that adversarial inputs can trick agents into bypassing security controls and exposing information they shouldn’t. The disclosure is notable because Salesforce has been aggressive in deploying agents—CEO Marc Benioff said agents now handle 50% of the company’s work.

Reports emerged of a malicious AI agent server stealing emails . The incident highlights how bad actors are already weaponizing agent infrastructure—creating rogue agents that exfiltrate data under the guise of legitimate AI services.

Additional research found that seemingly harmless photos could be used to hack AI agents . The attack technique involves embedding malicious instructions in images that agents process—bypassing text-based filters. TechRadar warned that IT can’t afford blind trust when agents go rogue.

CISOs Not Ready

Fast Company reported that AI agents are “breaking bad” and CISOs aren’t ready . The article documented how security teams lack visibility into agent behavior, can’t audit agent decisions, and don’t have tools to police agent-to-agent interactions. Help Net Security similarly noted that “AI agents are here, now comes the hard part for CISOs.”

Zscaler’s analysis examined the challenge of balancing speed and security in AI agent deployments—arguing that security can’t be an afterthought when agents have access to sensitive systems and data.

Computer Weekly asked whether AI agents are a blessing or curse for cybersecurity. The article noted that while agents can help defend systems, they also create new attack surfaces that defenders must monitor and protect.

Industry Response: New Security Platforms

The industry is responding with new security platforms and governance frameworks:

Astrix Security announced the first AI Agent Control Plane (ACP) for secure-by-design agent deployment. The ACP provides centralized visibility into agent permissions, data access, and connections—giving security teams a way to police agent behavior at scale. The Hacker News described how Astrix’s platform helps secure the “agentic era.”

Airia launched Agent Constraints , the industry’s first policy engine for centralized AI agent governance. The platform lets enterprises set guardrails on what agents can do, what data they can access, and how decisions are reviewed—addressing the control problem that plagues agent deployments.

Covasant launched an AI Agent Control Tower to “bring order to the chaotic enterprise AI landscape.” The platform provides visibility, governance, and management capabilities for enterprises running multiple agents from different vendors.

Geordie’s $6.5 million seed round for an AI agent security platform reflects growing investment in agent security as a category.

Lasso Platform employs AI agents to secure AI applications , using agent technology to police agent behavior—a “fight fire with fire” approach to security.

The Hacker News published guidance on how to gain control of AI agents and non-human identities, noting that traditional identity management approaches don’t work when agents create their own sub-identities and permissions.

CrowdStrike debuted threat-hunting AI agents and partnered with Salesforce on security solutions for AI agents and applications. The company is positioning itself as a security provider for the agentic era.

Wipro integrated Simbian’s AI agent into its managed security services, reflecting how security providers are incorporating agents into their operations.

AI Magazine reported on Boomi’s argument that AI agent governance “can’t wait”—arguing that enterprises need governance frameworks before deploying agents at scale.

The security developments in September reveal a tension: enterprises want to deploy agents quickly, but the security infrastructure is still catching up. The MCP vulnerabilities and data leak disclosures are setbacks, but the rapid response from security vendors suggests the industry is treating security seriously, not as an afterthought.

Governance and Control

As enterprises deploy hundreds of AI agents, they need infrastructure to manage, monitor, and control them at scale. September saw the emergence of governance platforms, observability tools, and enterprise infrastructure for agent management—the “pickaxes and shovels” layer of the agent boom.

Policy Engines & Control Planes

Airia’s Agent Constraints policy engine enables centralized AI agent governance by letting enterprises define what agents can and cannot do. The platform addresses a fundamental challenge: how do you set policy for autonomous systems that are designed to act independently?

Covasant’s AI Agent Control Tower provides visibility into agent behavior across the enterprise, giving administrators a single pane of glass to monitor and manage agents from different vendors.

OneTrust announced AI agents and new capabilities to deliver “AI-ready governance”—extending its privacy and compliance platform to handle AI agent deployments.

Observability & Monitoring

Monte Carlo launched Agent Observability to help teams build reliable AI systems. The platform provides monitoring, debugging, and quality assurance for AI agents—extending data observability to the agentic realm.

AWS Bedrock AgentCore Observability helps build trustworthy AI agents with monitoring tools that track agent decisions, data usage, and performance over time.

Temporal and OpenAI launched AI Agent Durability with a public preview integration that helps agents recover from failures and maintain state across long-running workflows.

Enterprise Infrastructure

Microsoft’s Agent Factory focuses on safe and secure agent development , providing a blueprint for enterprises building agents. The company also published guidance on connecting agents, apps, and data with open standards like MCP and A2A, and developer tools for rapid agent development .

Microsoft Marketplace promises simpler AI agent purchasing , giving enterprises a centralized way to discover and buy agent capabilities from multiple vendors.

The Cross App Access Protocol makes AI agents enterprise-ready by providing a standard way for agents to access applications across an enterprise without hard-coded integrations.

Salesforce’s MuleSoft Agent Fabric turns AI agents into enterprise infrastructure , providing integration and connectivity capabilities that let agents work with enterprise data and systems safely.

Deloitte published analysis arguing that scaling AI agents may be risky without an enterprise marketplace to help organizations discover, evaluate, and procure agent capabilities.

PwC published a guide on validating multi-agent AI systems , covering modular testing and system-level governance—a framework for ensuring agent reliability as systems grow complex.

The governance and control infrastructure emerging in September suggests enterprises are preparing for agent deployments at scale. Control planes, observability platforms, and standard protocols are the unsung infrastructure that makes large-scale agent deployments possible.

Industry Specialization

Agents are going vertical, with specialized applications emerging in healthcare, finance, customer service, logistics, automotive, and manufacturing.

Healthcare: Hyro launched ProActive Px with an AI agent to help healthcare organizations handle coverage disruption caused by OBBBA. Stanford HAI developed real-world benchmarks for healthcare AI agents , addressing the challenge of evaluating agent performance in medical settings.

Finance: Auquan released the first purpose-built AI agent for financial credit and deal analysis. LSEG and Databricks partnered to enable AI agent market data access , giving agents direct access to financial data sources. Revolut is building AI agents for sales, customer service, and more—extending the fintech’s automation capabilities.

Customer Service: Primary Health Solutions deployed SoundHound’s AI agent platform for enhanced patient experience. AT&T tested a new AI digital receptionist for visitor management.

Logistics: Deutsche Telekom’s logistics AI agent automates processes without requiring IT expertise—a no-code approach to agent deployment in logistics operations.

Automotive: Cerence AI is developing an AI agent for working on the go in vehicles, while AI Business reported on AI agents that promise to make working while in vehicles safer. One AI agent helps negotiate car deals , saving buyers time and money.

Real Estate: Citi is developing agents for real estate transactions, reflecting how financial services are exploring agent applications across their businesses.

Manufacturing: Kraft Heinz is piloting an AI agent to streamline ketchup production , showing how CPG companies are applying agents to manufacturing operations.

Pharma: AI agents are coming to pharma , with implications for clinical trials and drug development. McKinsey published analysis on reimagining life science enterprises with agentic AI.

Civil Engineering: An AI agent for civil design expanded into North America , automating aspects of engineering design work.

Legal: Artificial Lawyer hosted a webinar on AI agents and legal judgment, reflecting the legal industry’s exploration of agent applications.

Semiconductors: Semiconductor Engineering examined AI agents for UVM generation, highlighting challenges and opportunities in chip design automation.

The verticalization of agents reflects a maturing market. Rather than building general-purpose agent platforms, companies are creating specialized agents that understand industry workflows, terminology, and compliance requirements.

Developer Tools and Frameworks

Building AI agents requires new tools and frameworks. September saw a proliferation of developer resources, tutorials, and technical infrastructure for agent development.

LinkedIn published details on how it built enterprise multi-agent AI on existing messaging infrastructure—showing how to add agents to platforms without rip-and-replace.

NVIDIA released a tutorial on building a RAG agent with Nemotron , providing developers with code examples for retrieval-augmented generation agents.

Anthropic published a guide on effective context engineering for AI agents —a key technical challenge in agent development.

Hackster.io published a tutorial on building a local router AI-agent with n8n and llama.cpp , showing how to build agents that run locally rather than calling external APIs.

MarkTechPost argued that building AI agents is “5% AI and 100% software engineering” , emphasizing that agent development requires traditional software practices more than novel AI techniques.

AWS published guidance on accelerating AI agent development with the Nova Act IDE extension , providing developers with tools to build agents in Amazon’s ecosystem.

The New Stack published articles on spec-driven development as “the key to scalable AI agents” and AI agents and their life cycle —explaining what developers should know about agent lifecycle management.

KDnuggets published articles on 7 free web search APIs for AI agents and 12 essential lessons for building AI agents —providing practical resources for developers.

TechTarget published a guide to AI agent frameworks for evaluating agentic platforms and a LangChain tutorial for beginners.

CoinGecko published guides on building an AI agent with SendAI’s Solana Agent Kit and how to build your own crypto AI agent —reflecting interest in agents for cryptocurrency and blockchain applications.

Google published guidance on delighting users by combining ADK Agents with Fancy Frontends using AG-UI , helping developers build user interfaces for agent interactions.

Augment Code published a step-by-step guide to multi-file code refactoring with AI agents and a blog on automating customer feedback and support with AI agents .

MetalBear’s Mirrord gives AI agents a staging environment to test their code—addressing the challenge of safely testing agent-generated code.

Simplilearn published a guide to the best AI agents , reviewing top tools and frameworks.

SitePoint reviewed SmythOS as a solution for “stopping duct-taping AI agents together”—arguing that visual development tools can help manage agent complexity.

The technical ecosystem is maturing rapidly. Developers now have access to tutorials, frameworks, evaluation guides, and infrastructure tools that didn’t exist six months ago. This suggests the agent market is moving from experimental to production-grade development.

Testing and Evaluation

How do you know if an AI agent works? September brought significant developments in agent testing, evaluation, and validation.

Cresta launched automated AI agent testing so businesses can deploy AI agents with confidence. The platform provides automated testing capabilities that can validate agent behavior before production deployment.

Bluejay emerged as the startup behind the AI agent testing revolution , offering tools to evaluate agent performance and reliability.

Stanford’s real-world benchmarks for healthcare AI agents provide a way to evaluate agent performance in medical settings—addressing the lack of standardized evaluation metrics.

PwC’s guide on validating multi-agent AI systems covers modular testing and system-level governance, providing enterprises with a framework for ensuring agent reliability.

No Jitter published articles on consumer expectations for AI agent accuracy and ensuring AI agents have the best knowledge —highlighting that accuracy and knowledge quality are key adoption factors.

The emergence of testing and evaluation tools reflects the enterprise imperative to validate agent performance before trusting agents with customer-facing or business-critical tasks. As agents move from prototypes to production, the discipline of agent evaluation is becoming formalized.

What September Means

September 2025 marked a phase transition for AI agents—from concept to deployment, from experimental to essential. The developments of the month reveal five patterns shaping the agentic future.

1. Infrastructure First

The industry is building rails before running fast. Google’s payments protocol, Visa’s commerce tools, and the emergence of governance platforms all suggest that infrastructure is being laid before explosive adoption. This is the opposite of typical tech hype cycles—usually products come first, infrastructure second. The agent ecosystem is being built methodically, with payment protocols, security platforms, and governance frameworks emerging alongside the first generation of products.

2. Verticalization Wins

Investors are funding specific use cases, not general agent platforms. Sierra and Cognition are exceptions that prove the rule—horizontal platforms at eye-popping valuations. But most capital is flowing to vertical applications: accounting (uiAgent, Paid), finance (Tabs), retail (Envive), healthcare (Hyro), security (Geordie). The pattern suggests enterprises want agents that understand their industry, not general-purpose assistants that require extensive customization.

3. Security Is the Bottleneck

The MCP vulnerabilities and Salesforce data leaks are setbacks, but they’re also forcing the industry to take security seriously. The rapid emergence of security platforms (Astrix ACP, Airia Agent Constraints, Covasant Control Tower) suggests vendors are treating security as a product requirement, not an afterthought. The question is whether security can catch up to deployment speed—CISOs clearly aren’t ready, as Fast Company reported, but the tools to address the gap are appearing rapidly.

4. Enterprise Integration Is Key

Microsoft, Oracle, Workday, Amazon, Notion, Box, Adobe— incumbents are embedding agents into existing products, not selling standalone agent platforms. This approach reduces adoption friction but also raises questions about lock-in and interoperability. The Cross App Access Protocol and other standards suggest the industry recognizes the need for interoperability, but proprietary agent ecosystems may still emerge.

5. The Agentic Organization Is Emerging

McKinsey published “The agentic organization: contours of the next paradigm” and “One year of agentic AI: six lessons” , arguing that agents aren’t just tools—they’re changing how work gets done. MIT Sloan Management Review published “Agentic AI at scale: redefining management for a superhuman workforce” , examining how organizations must adapt to manage autonomous AI workers.

CIO published articles on “rethinking the IT organization for the agentic AI era” and “taming AI agents: the autonomous workforce of 2026” —reflecting how IT leaders are preparing for agent deployments.

Bessemer Venture Partners published an “AI agent autonomy scale” —a new way to understand use case maturity and agent capabilities.

SaaStr published a practical “AI Agent Playbook” documenting how the company deployed 20+ agents to scale 8-figure revenue with single-digit headcount. Another SaaStr article examined whether AI agents can really manage other agents —concluding that while agent-on-agent management is possible, it creates “more work, not less” in the near term.

Readiness Gaps and Failure Rates

DesignRush reported that over 40% of AI agent projects will fail —and offered strategies to beat the odds. The failure rate is typical for emerging technologies, but it suggests the agent honeymoon is ending and the hard work of proving ROI is beginning.

Financial Management magazine found that executives embrace AI agents despite readiness gaps—highlighting the tension between enthusiasm for agent capabilities and preparation for deployment challenges.

CIO reported that “AI agents are coming. Your data isn’t ready”—arguing that data infrastructure is a bottleneck for agent deployments.

HR Executive published multiple articles on the organizational implications of agents: “Why every AI agent needs a human manager and clear job description” , “5 things to think about before bringing AI agents into the organization” , and “AI agents: where are they now? From proof of concept to success stories” .

The World Economic Forum argued that agentic AI presents a turning point for business resilience—while The Economist published a warning from Meredith Whittaker that “AI agents are coming for your privacy.”

IT Pro published a skeptical take , arguing that businesses are being oversold on agent capabilities.

Looking Forward: What Comes Next

September’s developments suggest Q4 2025 will focus on three priorities:

  1. Governance: Enterprises that deployed agents experimentally in Q3 will build governance frameworks in Q4. Control planes, observability platforms, and policy engines will move from nice-to-have to must-have.

  2. Security Hardening: The MCP vulnerabilities will prompt security reviews across agent deployments. Expect enterprises to demand security certifications, penetration testing, and compliance audits before trusting agents with sensitive data.

  3. ROI Proof: With 40% of projects at risk of failure, enterprises will pressure vendors to prove ROI. Results-based pricing models (like Paid’s) will become more common as customers refuse to pay for agents that don’t deliver measurable outcomes.

The honeymoon period for AI agents is ending. September showed that the technology is real—funding is flowing, products are shipping, enterprises are deploying. But the honeymoon is ending, and now comes the hard work of making agents reliable, secure, and valuable at scale.

BCG noted that AI agents are transforming consumer goods, while IBM argued that designing workflows where humans and agents thrive is the key to successful deployment.

Japan’s Tokio Marine and OpenAI announced a partnership on developing AI agents—reflecting international interest in the technology beyond the US market.

The Times predicted “downloadable employees” as the next workforce revolution, while ITPro asked whether workers should prepare to become AI agent bosses.

CNBC reported that companies are spending big on agentic AI “without always knowing what it does”—highlighting the knowledge gap that still exists between agent vendors and enterprise buyers.

AIMultiple published “12 reasons AI agents still aren’t ready in 2026” , while Visionary Marketing offered “AI agents, beyond the hype” —both attempting to ground expectations in reality.

September 2025 was a landmark month for AI agents—not because any single breakthrough occurred, but because the technology moved from concept to deployment at enterprise scale. The funding, product launches, security vulnerabilities, and governance developments all point to an ecosystem that is growing up quickly. The question for Q4 is whether the industry can address the security, governance, and ROI challenges before enterprises lose patience with the experimentation phase.

The infrastructure is being built, the products are shipping, and the money is flowing. Now comes the hard part: making AI agents reliable enough to trust with business-critical work. September showed both the promise and the peril of the agentic future—progress is real, but so are the challenges ahead.

item.title: The AI Agent Wars: $20,000 Agents, Autonomous Systems, and Enterprise Platforms Battle for Supremacy

Every major tech company launched agent platforms, enterprises deployed agents at scale, and startups raised $93.8 million to solve critical infrastructure gaps.

item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 285 articles published between March 1, 2025 and April 1, 2025, surveying a pivotal month for AI agents. OpenAI plans to charge $20,000 monthly for “PhD-level” AI agents while China’s Manus demonstrates fully autonomous capabilities. Every major tech company launched agent platforms, enterprises deployed agents at scale, and startups raised $93.8 million to solve critical infrastructure gaps.

The $20,000 Question

OpenAI is reportedly planning to charge up to $20,000 per month for specialized AI agents designed to perform “PhD-level” research work, according to a report in The Information . The reported pricing strategy includes three tiers: $2,000 monthly for “high-income knowledge workers,” $10,000 for software development agents, and the $20,000 tier for research-intensive tasks requiring doctoral-level expertise.

The pricing is based on performance metrics from OpenAI’s o3 and o3-mini models, which use what the company calls “private chain of thought” reasoning. According to Ars Technica , o3 scored 87.5% on the ARC-AGI visual reasoning benchmark (comparable to the 85% human threshold), 96.7% on the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Exam (missing just one question), and 87.7% on GPQA Diamond, which contains graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry questions. On the Frontier Math benchmark by EpochAI, o3 solved 25.2% of problems while no other model has exceeded 2%.

The reported pricing represents a dramatic departure from current consumer AI costs. ChatGPT Plus remains $20 per month, Claude Pro costs $30 monthly, and even ChatGPT Pro’s $200/month subscription is tiny compared to the proposed enterprise fees. As xAI developer Hieu Pham noted in a widely-shared tweet: “most PhD students, including the brightest stars who can do way better work than any current LLMs—are not paid $20K / month.”

Behind the pricing strategy is significant financial pressure. OpenAI reportedly lost approximately $5 billion last year covering operational costs. At the same time, investor commitment remains strong: SoftBank has reportedly committed $3 billion to spend on OpenAI’s agent products this year alone.

Alongside the pricing news, OpenAI unveiled new tools for building AI agents, including a “reasoning” API that enables developers to build agents that can “think before they speak” using the company’s o3 models. The eWeek reported that these tools represent a “powerful suite” to simplify AI agent development.

However, skepticism about the “PhD-level” framing has emerged. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.” The models still struggle with confabulations—instances where they generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information—which remains a critical concern for research applications where accuracy matters.

The Autonomous Agent Arrival

While OpenAI focuses on premium pricing, a Chinese startup called Butterfly Effect has captured global attention with Manus, an AI agent described as the country’s first “fully autonomous” agent. According to Live Science , representatives claim Manus is “the world’s first general AI agent” designed to think, plan, and execute real-world tasks independently.

Unlike conventional AI tools that primarily assist users by providing recommendations or answering queries, Manus functions without human intervention . As The Economic Times explained , Manus “can come up with an itinerary for a trip to Japan, analyze stocks, and handle other complex tasks on its own.”

The emergence of Manus has drawn immediate comparisons to DeepSeek, another Chinese AI model that went viral earlier this year. As Axios reported , the new agent is “winning expert acclaim while stoking concern over another AI advance rooted in Chinese research and development.” Yicai Global claimed that Manus “is said to beat OpenAI’s Deep Research” in performance comparisons.

MIT Technology Review noted that researchers are actively testing Manus’s capabilities. The South China Morning Post reported that the startup’s founder believes Manus “transcends chatbots” in its ability to take independent action.

Manus added a mobile app and subscription plans in March, expanding access beyond web interfaces. Geeky Gadgets described how the agent is “redefining task automation and workflow management” through advanced automation, research, and coding capabilities.

The autonomous capabilities have also sparked discussion about how close we might be to artificial general intelligence (AGI). As Quartz noted , China now has a “completely autonomous” AI agent that operates differently from Western models. SiliconANGLE reported that the agent is “getting global attention for its autonomous smarts.”

Platform Wars: Big Tech’s Agent Offensive

March marked a coordinated offensive from every major technology company, each launching agent platforms aimed at enterprise dominance.

Microsoft: 400,000 Agents Deployed

Microsoft emerged as the early leader in the agent platform race. According to Cloud Wars , 160,000 customers have built 400,000 AI agents using the company’s Copilot platform. The scale demonstrates how quickly enterprises are moving beyond experimentation to deployment.

The company announced a range of specialized agents across different domains:

  • Security agents: Six new AI agents for security tasks, including phishing triage that can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks” and alert fatigue reduction that frees up human defenders
  • Factory automation: New agents for manufacturing environments announced at Hannover Messe 2025
  • Sales agents: AI Accelerator for Sales and new sales agents to accelerate AI-first selling
  • Research and data analysis: OpenAI-powered Copilot agents for workflow acceleration

Microsoft also expanded partnerships: Adobe joined to empower marketers with AI agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot, while OneTrust launched an AI agent built with Microsoft Security Copilot.

ZDNET reported on two new “deep reasoning” AI agents that can speed up workflows. The company is positioning its agents as alternatives to Salesforce CRM systems.

Amazon: Browser Control in Nova Act

Amazon entered the agent platform wars with Nova Act, an AI agent that can directly control web browsers to navigate websites and make purchases. According to The Verge , Amazon’s new agent “is designed to do your shopping.”

The browser-controlling capability represents a significant technical milestone. RetailWire reported that Nova Act “can take over a web browser and make purchases” on behalf of users. As PYMNTS noted , the agent can “shop and place orders” autonomously.

Beyond consumer applications, Amazon Web Services announced general availability of multi-agent collaboration on Bedrock, enabling multiple agents to work together on complex tasks. CNBC reported that the Nova launch “puts it up against rivals OpenAI, Anthropic.”

Salesforce: Agent Marketplace

Salesforce pursued an app store-style strategy with AgentExchange, a marketplace for AI agent skills launched with 200+ initial partners . As Techzine Global reported , the marketplace is “specifically focused on skill-sharing” between agents.

The company also launched Agentforce 2dx, which enables AI agents to run in the background rather than requiring explicit user prompts. According to Techzine Global , the update sets “a new standard” as “AI agents become proactive.”

InfoWorld noted that the update aims to simplify AI agent development and deployment. Salesforce DevOps reported that AgentExchange is designed to “drive adoption of role-based AI agents.”

In healthcare, Salesforce released pre-built AI agents to tackle “time-consuming healthcare tasks.”

Oracle: No-Code Agent Studio

Oracle introduced AI Agent Studio, a no-code tool for creating AI agents across its Fusion application suite. According to Oracle’s announcement , the studio is “available at no additional cost” and delivers “easy-to-use tools, including advanced testing, robust validation, and built-in security.”

ZDNET reported that the new tool is an “impressive next step for Oracle’s AI strategy.” Capacity Global noted that the studio enables businesses to “build custom AI agents.”

Oracle announced AI agents for financial crime detection, adding a “broad class of AI agents and agentic workflows” to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service. SiliconANGLE reported that customers can “create and modify AI agents across” the Fusion suite.

The company also announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform. As Techzine Global noted , Oracle is positioning Agent Studio for Fusion Cloud Applications.

ServiceNow: Pre-Built Agent Library

ServiceNow took a vertical-specific approach with its Yokohama platform release, which adds to “thousands of AI agents across CRM, HR, IT, and more,” according to the Business Wire announcement .

The company introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry . These agents, built with NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and DGX Cloud, are designed to “drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.”

Diginomica reported that Yokohama is “unleashing pre-configured AI agents, everywhere.” CX Today noted that ServiceNow is “going big on industry-specific innovation” with new AI agents and the Quality 360 acquisition.

Constellation Research reported that the Yokohama release “ups AI agent game” with ServiceNow Studio, an AI-powered workspace for no-code, low-code, and pro-code agent development. Techzine Global noted that ServiceNow is introducing “new AI agents for telecoms.”

Other Platform Players

Several other companies announced agent platforms:

  • PwC launched an AI agent operating system to “revolutionize AI workflows for enterprises”
  • Workato launched its enterprise AI agent platform and acquired AI customer support vendor DeepConverse
  • EY announced the EY.ai Agentic Platform , created with NVIDIA AI, for tax, risk, and finance domains
  • NVIDIA launched a family of open reasoning AI models for building agentic AI platforms
  • Kore.ai announced an agent platform for “building, deploying, and orchestrating agentic applications”
  • WSO2 expanded AI agent capabilities with platform-wide AI-native updates
  • Accenture debuted an AI agent builder within its AI Refinery platform
  • Deloitte unveiled Zora AI , described as “agentic AI for tomorrow’s workforce”
  • Adobe launched the Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator for businesses to activate AI agents

The Browser Pattern: Agents That Navigate the Web

A clear pattern emerged in March: browser-controlling agents as a primary interface for AI automation.

Browser Use raised $17 million in a funding round to help AI agents navigate websites. As TechCrunch explained , the startup is “making it easier for AI ‘agents’ to navigate websites.” SiliconANGLE reported that the funding will help “steer AI agents through the internet.”

Opera introduced “Browser Operator,” a native AI agent integrated directly into the browser to perform tasks for users. The screenshot from the announcement shows the agent designed to handle web-based workflows without leaving the browser.

Amazon’s Nova Act represents the most ambitious browser-controlling agent to date, with the ability to navigate websites and make purchases directly. The capability matters because it allows agents to interact with existing web infrastructure without requiring API integrations.

However, browser control also creates security concerns. Arcade.dev raised $12 million in seed funding specifically “to solve the biggest security problem with AI Agents.” As the company noted, it is “the first company to help AI agents securely take real-world actions on behalf of a user.”

Security Double-Edged: Agents as Defender and Threat

Agents as Defenders

Microsoft led the charge on using AI agents for security, announcing six specialized security agents for Security Copilot . According to The Verge , the agents will “help overwhelmed humans” by handling routine security tasks.

Help Net Security reported that the new AI agents “take on phishing, patching, alert fatigue.” The phishing triage agent specifically can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks, freeing up human defenders.”

SailPoint unveiled Harbor Pilot, a set of AI-powered agents for identity security . The agents are designed to “help identity teams work smarter, respond faster and secure their organizations more efficiently.”

Alpha Vision announced it will showcase AI agent-powered security solutions at ISC West 2025, demonstrating how agents can enhance physical security.

Oracle brought AI agents to financial crime detection , adding agents and agentic workflows to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.

Agents as Attackers

But security researchers also demonstrated how AI agents can be used maliciously. SC Media reported that OpenAI’s Operator AI agent “can be used in phishing attacks.” Researchers showed that the same browser-controlling capabilities that make agents useful for legitimate tasks also enable them to conduct autonomous phishing attacks .

The dual-use nature of agent capabilities creates a security dilemma. As Arcade.dev noted in its funding announcement, securely enabling AI agents to “take real-world actions on behalf of a user” is one of the most critical challenges facing the industry.

Vertical Agents: Healthcare, Finance, and Beyond

Healthcare

Salesforce released pre-built AI agents specifically designed to “tackle time-consuming healthcare tasks.” The agents target administrative workflows that consume provider time.

Wipro announced AI agent solutions for healthcare transformation , powered by Salesforce’s Agentforce platform.

Nature published a paper on “coordinated AI agents for advancing healthcare,” exploring how multi-agent systems can improve medical workflows.

Financial Services

Auquan launched an industry-first AI agent purpose-built for risk monitoring in financial services. As Corporate Compliance Insights noted , Auquan launched an “agentic AI risk agent for FinServ.”

Oscilar announced how it is transforming risk decisioning with AI agents, targeting financial risk assessment workflows.

Oracle expanded its financial crime detection agents , adding a broad class of AI agents to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.

Other Industries

Telecommunications: ServiceNow introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry , designed to drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.

Manufacturing: Microsoft launched new AI agents for factory automation at Hannover Messe 2025. Ford is using agents with NVIDIA for distributed inference with collaborative AI agents.

Real Estate: An AI agent claiming to be the “world’s first AI real estate agent” has generated $100M in sales . As The Express Tribune reported , the agent generated $100M in sales for Portugal real estate.

Retail: A Salesforce report found that 75% of retailers say AI agents will be “essential by 2026.” Amazon’s Nova Act directly targets retail shopping workflows.

Infrastructure Funding: Building the Agent Stack

Startup funding in March reveals where the agent ecosystem needs work. Infrastructure startups raised $93.8 million across several categories:

Browser Control & Security

  • Browser Use: Raised $17M for web navigation infrastructure
  • Arcade.dev: Raised $12M to solve agent security problems

Compliance & Payments

  • Norm Ai: Raised $48M for compliance automation agents
  • Paid: Raised $10.8M to “scale financial infrastructure for AI agents”

Specialized Infrastructure

  • Tiga.ai: Raised $2M to launch an AI agent for custom buying signals
  • Nunu.ai: Secured $6M to scale AI agents for game QA testing

Agent Monetization

  • Manny Medina (former Outreach CEO) launched a new startup tackling AI agent monetization. As TechCrunch noted , the startup “helps AI agents get paid.”

Platform Plays

Several consulting firms and platforms launched agent offerings:

  • Powered_by launched the “world’s first AI agency for SMBs” to help small businesses deploy agents
  • Tarka raised funding to arm go-to-market teams with AI agents
  • Oracle announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform
  • Adobe launched Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator

Reality Check: Why Agents Struggle

Despite the platform launches and funding, critical voices reminded the industry that significant challenges remain.

A widely-cited article titled “Why AI Agents Suck So Bad” detailed frustrating experiences with support agents, highlighting “limitations of current RAG-based AI systems in handling complex customer” issues.

More than half of companies have already deployed autonomous AI agents, according to a study by PagerDuty covered by Quartz. But adoption doesn’t equal satisfaction—implementation challenges abound.

CIO reported that IT leaders are “bracing for the AI agent management challenge.” As organizations deploy more agents, managing them becomes increasingly complex.

Skepticism about “PhD-level” marketing claims continues. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.”

Hidden risks in agent adoption are emerging, including concerns about data silos impacting agent performance. Enterprises face real management complexity as agent deployments scale.

What This Month Means

March 2025 was when AI agents graduated from research project to product. The evidence is across several dimensions:

Pricing as value signal: OpenAI’s reported $20,000 monthly pricing suggests the company believes these systems can deliver substantial enterprise value—even if the “PhD-level” framing remains marketing rhetoric.

Autonomous capabilities are here: China’s Manus demonstrated what fully autonomous agents can do, planning complex tasks without human intervention and drawing comparisons to DeepSeek’s viral impact.

Platform ubiquity: Every major tech company—Microsoft, Amazon, Salesforce, Oracle, ServiceNow—now offers an agent platform. The land grab for enterprise mindshare is underway.

Infrastructure being built: Startup funding of $93.8 million in a single month shows where the ecosystem needs work: browser control, security, payments, compliance, and monitoring.

Enterprise adoption accelerating: Microsoft’s 400,000 agents built by 160,000 customers, the PagerDuty study finding more than half of companies using autonomous agents, and industry-specific deployments all point to real adoption.

But we’re still early. Reliability issues persist, management complexity is real, and the gap between marketing claims and actual capabilities—especially around “PhD-level” performance—remains significant.

The next 6-12 months will be about deployment at scale. Which platforms actually deliver value? Which use cases prove durable? The agent wars have begun, but the winner is far from determined.
